one_liner: Pure-Go SQLite-dialect engine on its own columnar format; JIT filter/aggregate kernels beat C SQLite on read-mostly scans.
what_it_does: musql is a from-scratch SQLite-compatible SQL engine in pure Go (no cgo). It is used through database/sql (registers as `sqlite`), through the `musqld` server that speaks Turso's Hrana protocol, or through its `engine` package directly. It runs SQLite's SQL dialect but not SQLite's file format: data lives in a `.musq` columnar segment file plus an append-only delta, and existing `.db` files must be converted with `musql-convert`. It also ships CRDT and leader replication, FTS, R-tree and JSON.
how_it_is_fast: Most of the win comes from the storage layout. Fixed-width columns are stored contiguously, so a filter reads one `[]int64` block instead of walking SQLite's varint record headers and b-tree cell pointers (format-design.md measures 2.1 ns/row against SQLite's 114 ns/row format floor). A peephole pass (`segment_peephole.go`) spots filter-and-count, sum-over-filter, GROUP BY and ORDER BY ... LIMIT shapes in the compiled VDBE program and adds guarded fast-path opcodes. These call machine code that `internal/jit` emits at run time: AVX2 four-lane or NEON two-lane compare kernels, with a scalar fallback, mapped W^X (mmap RW, copy, mprotect RX) and entered through one Go-assembly trampoline per architecture. Bare `count(*)` is answered from the segments' recorded row counts, and top-N runs a bounded heap over an int64 block.
when_to_use: Embedded, read-mostly Go applications that run many integer range-filter counts or sums over a table of about 100k rows or more: one-predicate filtered count 28 us vs C SQLite 2.17 ms on Apple M4, 89 us vs 6.19 ms on a Xeon D-2123IT (engine-direct API).
Simple integer GROUP BY aggregates and `ORDER BY col DESC LIMIT n` top-N over large tables (2.0-2.7x vs C SQLite).
Projects that need SQLite SQL without cgo (cross-compiles to the Go GOOS/GOARCH matrix) and accept a separate on-disk format.
Teams already on Turso/libSQL clients who want a self-hosted Hrana server, where musql's reads also beat Turso's Go driver in the published table.
when_not_to_use: Any query shape the recogniser does not model: min/max, BETWEEN, OR, IN lists, IS NULL, LIKE, text ordering, DISTINCT, subqueries, EXISTS, UNION and OFFSET run the ordinary VDBE, which the harness's own comments put at about 3.5x slower than C SQLite on a scan. These shapes were left out of the published table.

Write-heavy workloads: the harness calls writes the engine's worst side and the published run skipped them. write-path-overlay.md measured 3,442 MB allocated for one bulk UPDATE over about 10k rows, with GC drain at 39% of CPU before cuts.
Point lookups and indexed joins: rowid lookup 1.8x slower, secondary-index equality 2.9x slower and equi-join 1.3x slower than C SQLite on the Xeon.
Applications that must open existing SQLite .db files in place or share them with C SQLite processes: conversion is required, and multi-process concurrency against a live C writer is not claimed.
Production use that needs maturity: one squashed commit (2026-10-05), 29 stars, and a run-time code generator whose linux/arm64 path format-design.md says had never run on hardware when written.

integration.form: Go module (`go get github.com/samyfodil/musql/driver`), plus musqld server binary or Docker image
integration.dependencies: github.com/coder/websocket, golang.org/x/sys, google.golang.org/protobuf; no cgo (the benchmark/differential harness is a separate module that needs cgo for mattn/go-sqlite3)
integration.platforms: Any Go target for the engine; JIT kernels only on amd64 and arm64 under linux or darwin (AVX2 vector kernel on amd64, scalar kernel without AVX2, NEON on arm64); exercised on darwin/arm64 and amd64, linux/arm64 builds but was untested per format-design.md
integration.thread_safety: database/sql semantics; two musql connections in one process are covered by TestN4ConcurrentReadersAndWriters, cross-process concurrency with a live C SQLite writer is not claimed; README asks for one SQL statement per Exec/Query call
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: SQL dialect and database/sql driver name match (import swap), but data must be converted to .musq and the JIT speedups apply only to a few read shapes

gotchas: Harness finding: the published musql column is the engine-direct API (`musqlengine.Open` + `ReadOnlyPager.QueryArgs`, returning raw Values), while C SQLite is timed through database/sql, cgo and fmt-rendered strings. The harness also times a musql arm through database/sql (the API the README tells users to adopt), but docs/benchmarks.md does not publish that column. format-design.md section 8b measured the driver's per-statement cost at about 0.2 ms at an earlier stage and said it dwarfs the 44 us kernel, so the 70-92x filtered-count wins should not be expected through database/sql (derived from page data: about 0.2 ms plus 28 us against C's 2.17 ms would be roughly 9-10x on M4, if that older overhead figure still holds; no current driver numbers are published).

Speedups fall off a cliff when a query leaves the recognised shape. The same one-predicate count takes 9.83 ms with the fast path off vs 2.17 ms for C on M4. A bare `count(*)` falls back to 74.5 ms (M4) and 276.8 ms (Xeon) against C's 9 us and 47 us, because without the segment row-count shortcut the VDBE decodes every row. Small SQL edits such as BETWEEN for a range or an added OR move a query off the fast path.

The published run sets BENCH_SKIP to drop 17 read shapes (including min/max and BETWEEN, which sit next to the winning shapes) and all writes. C SQLite is opened with driver defaults (no cache_size or mmap_size PRAGMA), so it is an untuned baseline. The page says each workload is checked on 40 bind values before timing; in the code the check loop runs after the timing loop (5-40 values by cost) and is fatal before the table prints, so published tables did pass it.

The JIT writes machine code into mmap'd memory and jumps into it from Go through hand-written trampolines (Go's frame and LR conventions on arm64, X18 reserved on darwin). That is an unsafe surface in an otherwise memory-safe codebase, and design notes record several fast paths that silently declined or returned wrong cells until the counters and value-by-value differential checks were added.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick musql over pg_jitter, AsmJit-backed or sljit-backed PostgreSQL JITs when you need an embedded, cgo-free SQLite-dialect store in Go and your hot queries are integer filter/count/sum, GROUP BY or top-N over read-mostly data. Use those PostgreSQL JITs if you are on PostgreSQL, and stay on C SQLite for point lookups, joins, writes or arbitrary SQL shapes.
verified_claims_summary: The author's harness TestBenchColumnarVsC ran 100,000-row, disk-backed, warm-cache reads, timed for about 200 ms each, with every arm's answers checked against C SQLite (mattn/go-sqlite3 v1.14.48, Go 1.27 toolchain per go.mod). On Apple M4 and Intel Xeon D-2123IT, musql's engine-direct API with its JIT beat C SQLite 65-92x on integer filtered counts, 7.6-8.5x on sum over a filter, 2.0-2.7x on GROUP BY and top-N, and 1.6-1.8x on whole-table count. It was at parity or 1.2-2.9x slower on rowid, secondary-index and join lookups, with non-JIT shapes and writes excluded from the run.
status_note: Active but very young: published as a single squashed commit on 2026-10-05, 29 stars, Apache-2.0, pure Go and easy to vendor. It has a strong differential-testing culture (67,800-73,855 SQLite test-suite statements with zero wrong results), but treat it as a fast path for a narrow set of read shapes on converted data, not as a general SQLite replacement.
